[1] Foreword Predicting the future is fraught with risk, but the greater risk is in failing to plan for our destiny

[2] As a nation, we face a choice: to drift into our future or to actively shape it

[3] That is why I commissioned the Australia in the Asian Century White Paper

[4] I took a clear decision that our nation should actively plan for and shape our national future

[5] Only by doing so can we realise our vision of being a land of increased opportunity, prosperity and fairness

[6] Whatever else this century brings, it will bring Asia’s rise

[7] The transformation of the Asian region into the economic powerhouse of the world is not only unstoppable, it is gathering pace

[8] In this century, the region in which we live will become home to most of the world’s middle class

[9] Our region will be the world’s largest producer of goods and services and the largest consumer of them

[10] History teaches us that as economic weight shifts, so does strategic weight

[11] Thriving in the Asian century therefore requires our nation to have a clear plan to seize the economic opportunities that will flow and manage the strategic challenges that will arise

[12] There are also great social and cultural benefits to be had from broadening and deepening our people-to-people links across the region

[13] Our nation has benefited from Asia’s appetite for raw materials and energy

[14] The challenge we must now address is how Australia can benefit from what Asia will need next

[15] Australians do not come to these tasks empty-handed

[16] Our economy is strong because over the past 30 years we have been prepared to do the things that are necessary to build for tomorrow

[17] This approach has given us 21 years of continuous economic growth

[18] As a nation we pulled together during the Global Financial Crisis to successfully avoid recession and the loss of hundreds of thousands of jobs

[19] As a result of our courage to shape the future and our decisive action during the Global Financial Crisis we come to this century of change with economic strength

[20] iii Government has shown the fortitude to identify the right changes and get them done, in order to give us a more prosperous tomorrow

[21] We also have the benefits that come from a track record of engagement with the nations of our region

[22] Our principal relationships with China, India, Indonesia, Japan and the Republic of Korea have strengthened in recent years

[23] Our alliance with the United States remains as strong as ever

[24] Our institutional regional engagement combines the ongoing strength of the Asia–Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum with the now-developing East Asia Summit

[25] Our people-to-people links are also expanding as business, travel, communications and study relationships in our region continue to grow

[26] But we must build on all of these strengths combined if we are to seize the opportunities of the Asian century

[27] I want our nation to be a winner as our region changes and I want every Australian to be a winner too

[28] Put simply, as a Labor Prime Minister I want the new opportunities that will come in this century to be seized and shared

[29] I want us to take an approach to the looming change that is farsighted and focused on fairness

[30] This White Paper is a plan to build on our strengths and shape our future

[31] It details how, by 2025, Australia can be a winner in this Asian century by becoming more prosperous, more resilient, and sharing the new opportunities

[32] It calls on all of us to play our part in becoming a more Asia-literate and Asia-capable nation

[33] The Australian Government will play its part in leading our nation to this vision of the future during a time of enormous change

[34] Like past Labor governments, we will manage and shape change with the aim of providing better opportunities for all

[35] I commend this White Paper to you and ask you to play your part in shaping our future

[55] Executive summary Asia’s rise is changing the world

[56] This is a defining feature of the 21st century—the Asian century

[57] These developments have profound implications for people everywhere

[58] Asia’s extraordinary ascent has already changed the Australian economy, society and strategic environment

[59] The scale and pace of the change still to come mean Australia is entering a truly transformative period in our history

[60] Within only a few years, Asia will not only be the world’s largest producer of goods and services, it will also be the world’s largest consumer of them

[61] It is already the most populous region in the world

[62] In the future, it will also be home to the majority of the world’s middle class

[63] The Asian century is an Australian opportunity

[64] As the global centre of gravity shifts to our region, the tyranny of distance is being replaced by the prospects of proximity

[65] Australia is located in the right place at the right time—in the Asian region in the Asian century

[66] For several decades, Australian businesses, exporters and the community have grown their footprint across the region

[67] Today, for Australia, the minerals and energy boom is the most visible, but not the only, aspect of Asia’s rise

[68] As the century unfolds, the growth in our region will impact on almost all of our economy and society

[69] An increasingly wealthy and mobile middle class is emerging in the region, creating new opportunities

[70] They are demanding a diverse range of goods and services, from health and aged care to education to household goods, and tourism, banking and financial services, as well as high-quality food products

[71] Beyond economic gains, there are many valuable opportunities for building stronger relationships across the region, including through closer educational, cultural and people-to-people links

[72] Our nation also has the strength that comes from a long history of engagement with countries in Asia

[73] Australia’s relationships in our region are strong and robust, including with Asian nations like China, Japan, India, Indonesia and the Republic of Korea (South Korea

[74] But in this Asian century we must enter a new phase of deeper and broader engagement

[75] This White Paper provides a roadmap for the whole of Australia—governments, business, unions, and the broader community—in this next phase

[76] Our goal is to secure Australia as a more prosperous and resilient nation that is fully part of our region and open to the world

[77] Australia starts from a position of strength

[78] Just as our region has a lot to offer us, we have a lot to offer our region

[79] We have strong, world-leading institutions, a multicultural and highly skilled workforce, and a productive, open and resilient 2 economy, which is one of the strongest in the world

[80] These assets have been reinforced by a series of economic reforms and good decisions made over past decades, including Australia’s world-beating actions to avoid the worst impacts of the Global Financial Crisis

[81] Our strengths have long been reflected in Australia’s interaction with countries in Asia

[82] Over the past 50 years, Australia’s trade with Asia as a share of our total trade has risen dramatically

[83] Our financial, political and cultural links have deepened

[84] We have strong relationships and close friendships with countries across the region

[85] But Australia’s success will be based on choice, not chance

[86] In order to succeed, we must sustain the policy settings and pathways that have served us well

[87] We need to reinforce our strong social foundations, including our national institutions, our cultural diversity and our outward-looking society

[88] We will need to do more than this—we all need to respond to the rapid changes occurring in our region

[89] Australians need to act in five key areas in order to succeed in the Asian century

[90] First, irrespective of how the Asian century evolves, Australia’s prosperity will come from building on our strengths

[91] We need to reinforce the foundations of our fair society and our prosperous, open and resilient economy at home

[92] We need to build on areas where we already perform well, in order to extend our comparative advantage

[93] Critical to this will be ongoing reform and investment across the five pillars of productivity—skills and education, innovation, infrastructure, tax reform and regulatory reform

[94] Second, as a nation we must do even more to develop the capabilities that will help Australia succeed

[95] Our greatest responsibility is to invest in our people through skills and education to drive Australia’s productivity performance and ensure that all Australians can participate and contribute

[96] Capabilities that are particularly important for the Asian century include job-specific skills, scientific and technical excellence, adaptability and resilience

[97] Using creativity and design-based thinking to solve complex problems is a distinctive Australian strength that can help to meet the emerging challenges of this century

[98] As a nation we also need to broaden and deepen our understanding of Asian cultures and languages, to become more Asia literate

[99] These capabilities are needed to build stronger connections and partnerships across the region

[100] Third, Australia’s commercial success in the region requires that highly innovative, competitive Australian firms and institutions develop collaborative relationships with others in the region

[101] Australian firms need new business models and new mindsets to operate and connect with Asian markets

[102] We will work to make the region more open and integrated, encouraging trade, investment and partnerships

[103] Firms will adapt their business models to seize the opportunities created in our region

[104] Fourth, Australia’s future is irrevocably tied to the stability and sustainable security of our diverse region

[105] Australia has much to offer through cooperation with other nations to support sustainable security in the region

[106] We will work to build trust and cooperation, bilaterally and through existing regional mechanisms

[107] We will continue to support a greater role for Asian countries in a rules-based regional and global order

[108] Australia’s alliance with the United States and a strong US presence in Asia will support regional stability, as will China’s full participation in regional developments

[109] Fifth, we need to strengthen Australia’s deep and broad relationships across the region at every level

[110] These links are social and cultural as much as they are political and economic

[111] Improving people-to-people links can unlock large economic and social gains

[112] While the Australian Government plays a leading role in strengthening and building relationships with partners in the region—with more intensive diplomacy across Asia—others across a broad spectrum spanning business, unions, community groups and educational and cultural institutions also play an important role

[113] Stronger relationships will lead to more Australians having a deeper understanding of what is happening in Asia and being able to access the benefits of growth in our region

[114] In turn, more of our neighbours in the region will know us better than they do today

[115] Success in the Asian century requires a whole-of-Australia effort, with businesses, unions, communities and governments being partners in a transformation as profound as any that have defined Australia throughout our history

[116] It is in the interests of all Australians—and therefore in the national interest—to develop the capabilities and connections that Australia will need, so that we can contribute to, and learn from, the region, and take full advantage of these opportunities

[117] The challenges ahead require sustained effort; Australians cannot build stronger relationships or learn new skills overnight, or even over five years, especially given the diversity of the countries in our region

[118] Some actions can be taken immediately, but others require further conversation among communities across the nation, detailed planning and careful implementation over a generation

[126] In the past 20 years, China and India have almost tripled their share of the global economy and increased their absolute economic size almost six times over

[127] By 2025, the region as a whole will account for almost half the world’s output

[128] Many millions of people will have been lifted out of poverty

[129] They will live longer and be better connected to the world

[130] Chart 1: Asia’s economic resurgence is set to continue Asia’s ability to capitalise on open global markets for goods and services has been crucial to its economic transformation

[131] Central to this has been a widespread commitment to investing in people and physical capital

[132] Asia continues to develop against a backdrop of persistent global challenges

[133] First among these is the present weakness in major advanced economies, where more moderate economic growth is expected

[134] Second, there are global challenges such as climate change and other emerging challenges in the areas of food, water and energy security

[135] Third, Asia has policy challenges of its own, including the continuation of market-based reforms to promote economically and environmentally sustainable growth, dealing with urbanisation, ageing populations in some countries and developing social safety nets

[140] The United States will remain the most powerful strategic actor in Asia for the foreseeable future

[141] But the economic growth and broader international interests of Asia’s large powers, especially China and India, are changing the established strategic order

[142] Rising national wealth is allowing states to modernise their defence forces, to acquire more advanced capabilities and to project power

[143] At the same time, economic growth will put more pressure on energy, water and food resources

[144] Existing regional strategic tensions remain, such as North Korea’s nuclear program and unresolved territorial disputes

[145] Australia’s strategic landscape is becoming more crowded and complex

[146] The stability and prosperity of our region will depend on how major-power relations evolve, particularly between China, India, Japan and the United States

[147] A degree of competition is inevitable as Asia’s strategic order changes

[148] But all countries in the region have a deep investment in stability and economic growth: the complex interdependencies and growing bilateral engagement are strong stabilising forces

[149] Still, while the likelihood of miscalculation may be low, the potential consequences would be high

[150] These risks are driving bilateral and regional efforts to build trust, dialogue and habits of cooperation in the region, and those efforts are explored in this White Paper

[151] Australia in Asia Australia is in a good position to make the most of the opportunities that will flow from the Asian century

[152] Despite uneven conditions across sectors, Australia has one of the strongest economies in the world and a bright outlook

[153] Unemployment is low

[154] Inflation is contained

[155] The terms of trade are high

[156] While commodity prices appear to have passed their record peak, considerable minerals and energy investment is still to come and large-scale production and exports are yet to flow

[157] Australia’s public finances are among the strongest in the world

[158] Government debt is low

[159] Our financial institutions are sound and we have the highest possible sovereign credit rating

[160] We have a multicultural, highly skilled and creative population that has demonstrated capabilities in innovation and complex problem solving

[161] We have vast natural resources and the know-how and technologies to develop them

[162] Australia’s foreign policy and strategic frameworks have built strong relationships in the region, enabling us to influence regional and, at times, global outcomes

[163] While Australia has many strengths, we will need to take action to ensure we continually adapt to the rapid changes in our region and transitions in our own economy

[164] Over the past decade, Asia’s demand for Australia’s natural resources has created a once-in-a-lifetime surge in our terms of trade and an extraordinary boom in minerals and energy investment

[165] This delivered a substantial increase in national income, even though productivity growth has been modest over the past decade. 8 While Australia’s terms of trade are expected to remain high for some time yet, productivity growth remains critical to lifting living standards in Australia

[166] This requires growth that is broadly based and sustainable

[167] Our goal is to ensure that Australians have higher incomes in a more diverse economy that is resilient in the face of ongoing change

[168] The Asian century offers a wealth of opportunities and career choices in a variety of businesses (including small and medium-sized enterprises), especially for Australia’s young people: • in mining and resource related sectors—continued economic development in the region will drive demand for energy and mineral resources • in tourism, sport, education, the arts and creative industries, professional, banking and financial services, and science and technology—thanks to growing affluence in Asia • in agriculture—rising food demand, connected to rising populations and an expanding middle class in Asia, offers an opportunity for Australia to be an important supplier of high-value food, requiring greater investment by agribusinesses to boost output and research, adapt to regulatory change and build capacity • in manufacturing and services—as Australian businesses join regional and global value chains and over time become increasingly integrated and specialised, they will offer high-value and innovative products and services • in environmentally sustainable growth, natural resource management, infrastructure development, urban design and health and aged care—as Australians leverage their expertise to do business with their neighbours

[169] To seize these opportunities, Australia must create deeper connections with Asia to broaden the flow of ideas and acquire new knowledge and capabilities

[170] Asia is an important source of new ideas, arts and culture, technologies and leading-edge science

[171] Australia stands to benefit greatly from Asia’s advance

[172] Increasingly, we look to measure our performance against standards of excellence in the region

[173] The arts, culture and creativity can broaden and strengthen Australia’s relationships in Asia, both formally and informally

[174] Australia’s cultural strengths—as home to the world’s oldest living culture, and as a country that welcomes diversity—underpin values of respect, understanding and inclusion that help to connect people, business, institutions and governments

[175] Two-way people movements between Australia and the rest of the region will further strengthen the fabric of Australian society and our way of life

[176] Australia is well positioned to continue attracting highly skilled and talented people from the region to live, study and work in Australia—just as Australians have much to offer the region in return

[177] Not all parts of the Australian economy are facing the same opportunities at the present time; some industries and regions are working through difficult transitions

[178] The Government, in partnership with business, unions and the wider community, is committed to targeted support for sectors and regions in transition, including by improving skills and education and helping with access to domestic and international markets

[179] As some business models are challenged, new development opportunities are opening up in other areas

[180] Australia’s regions make an important contribution to the economic, social and environmental fabric of our nation

[181] Regional Australia is home to around one-third of our population

[182] Primary industries, which are concentrated in regional Australia, make up close to two-thirds of our exports

[183] Strong demand from Asia will support development across northern Australia from Western Australia to Queensland, including in Darwin, and in other regions including Tasmania and the Upper Spencer Gulf

[184] Australia has a track record of managing immense structural adjustments more effectively than many other countries

[185] But the scale of change and opportunity presented by the Asian century is large and enduring; it requires a whole-of-Australia effort across the whole federation

[186] Businesses, communities and institutions all need to lead their own responses to the changing global economy

[187] All of us will need to work smarter to maximise prosperity and manage challenges well

[188] For the Government, that means continuing what we have done in recent years, by making the right decisions and continuing the proud tradition of reform that has spanned decades

[189] Twenty-five national objectives for 2025: a roadmap to navigate the Asian century The rise of Asia provides great opportunities for Australia

[190] To achieve the vision of a more prosperous and resilient Australia, fully part of the Asian region and open to the world, the Government has identified 25 objectives for the nation for

[191] These national objectives are set out in detail below, along with policy pathways to guide their achievement

[192] A productive and resilient Australian economy (Chapter 5) Together, the objectives and pathways in the roadmap provide mechanisms to strengthen Australia’s economy and society

[193] •

[194] By 2025, Australia’s GDP per person will be in the world’s top 10, up from 13th in 2011, requiring a lift in our productivity

[195] •

[196] This will mean Australia’s average real national income will be about $73,000 per person in 2025 compared with about $62,000 in

[197] Skills and education

[198] All Australians will have the opportunity to acquire the skills and education they need to participate fully in a strong economy and a fairer society

[199] •

[200] Australia’s school systems will be in the top five schooling systems in the world and our universities and training systems will be among the world’s best

[201] Pathways 

[202] Improve Australia’s early childhood education, schools, universities and training systems as strong foundations for building capability to improve productivity and connections with Asian nations (the full set of pathways is in national objectives 9–13 below

[203] 

[204] Increase participation among groups currently under-represented in the workforce, including through education and training, child care, paid parental leave, employment services and assistance for older Australians, so that more Australians can benefit from the Asian century

[205] 

[206] Continue to develop, through the Fair Work Act 2009, and ongoing partnership, a workforce culture in which employees, employers and unions collaborate for continuous improvement and productivity growth

[207] Innovation

[208] Australia will have an innovation system, in the top 10 globally, that supports excellence and dynamism in business with a creative problem-solving culture that enhances our evolving areas of strength and attracts top researchers, companies and global partnerships

[209] Pathways 

[210] Through the Industry and Innovation Statement, articulate an ambitious industry and innovation policy agenda for Australian business to create new jobs and seize new market opportunities

[211] 

[212] Through the National Research Investment Plan, provide a framework for investment in Australia’s scientific capabilities—including our research infrastructure, Australia’s workforce and fostering globalisation—to sustain our ability to help address the global challenges we and the region face

[213] 

[214] Improve financing options for Australia’s innovation system to make it easier to attract private investment, encourage entrepreneurship, build on government investment in science and technology and commercialise our ideas

[215] 

[216] Support collaboration across business, the research sector and governments to build scale and capability that encourages innovation, allowing Australia to make the most of emerging opportunities in the Asian region

[217] 

[218] Support Australian researchers to broaden and strengthen their partnerships with the region as Asia grows as a global science and innovation hub

[219] Infrastructure

[220] Australia will implement a systematic national framework for developing, financing and maintaining nationally significant infrastructure that will assist governments and the private sector to plan and prioritise infrastructure needs at least 20 years ahead

[221] •

[222] Infrastructure investment will support Australia’s growing trade and investment with the region, improve productivity and will reduce future congestion costs by billions of dollars a year

[223] Pathways 

[224] Work, including through Infrastructure Australia, with States and Territories, the private sector and academic institutions, to expand existing infrastructure plans by creating a long-term national infrastructure strategy that focuses on corridor planning, cross-jurisdictional networks and projects of national significance

[225] 

[226] Work with States and Territories to increase private sector involvement in new infrastructure projects, including removing barriers to investors (including superannuation funds) participating in infrastructure financing, and consider alternative ways to speed up project delivery

[227] 

[228] Improve the productivity, amenity and liveability of Australia’s cities by helping provide transparent and forward-looking analysis to support the States and Territories to deliver on their responsibilities, through forums such as the Standing Council on Transport and Infrastructure

[229] 

[230] Sharpen rules governing infrastructure provision and use, including by promoting greater competition in retail energy markets, ensuring energy network investment is efficient and avoiding unnecessary costs, as outlined in our forthcoming Energy White Paper, and reviewing third-party access regulation

[231] 4.

[232] Australia’s communications infrastructure and markets will be world leading and support the rapid exchange and spread of ideas and commerce in the Asian region

[233] •

[234] The National Broadband Network (NBN) will have bridged geographical barriers to Asian markets, allowing all Australian businesses and households to conduct more of their activities online

[235] •

[236] All Australians will have access to high-speed broadband through a nationwide fibre network and wireless satellite services

[237] •

[238] Australia will have high-speed broadband fibre to 93 per cent of premises, rolled out progressively to 2021 and capable of supporting speeds of one gigabit per second

[239] Pathways 

[240] Complete the rollout of the NBN to enhance digital commerce and productivity and boost trade and wider economic ties with Asia

[241] 

[242] Review and examine regulatory and other barriers to expanding into new technological markets, including through increased use of the NBN

[243] Tax system

[244] Australia’s tax and transfer system will be efficient and fair, encouraging continued investment in the capital base and greater participation in the workforce, while delivering sustainable revenues to support economic growth by meeting public and social needs

[245] Pathways 

[246] Ensure the tax system continues to support businesses to invest and adapt to take advantage of the Asian century, including through measures like the loss carry-back for companies and simpler tax arrangements for small business such as the immediate deduction for assets costing less than $6,500. 

[247] Ensure that the tax, transfer and superannuation system encourages Australians, particularly older Australians, to participate in the workforce and provides access to a minimum standard of living in retirement

[248] 

[249] Lift the tax-free threshold to at least $21,000, freeing more Australians from having to lodge a tax return and raising participation in the labour market

[250] 

[251] Facilitate State and Territory-led tax reform, to phase out their inefficient taxes and make better use of their efficient tax bases, including through processes like the State tax plan being developed by the New South Wales and South Australian Treasurers

[252] 

[253] Establish the Tax Studies Institute to provide policy-relevant research that will inform debate about tax reform goals and transitional pathways and provide opportunities for regional collaboration and exchange

[254] 

[255] Continue the national conversation about tax reform with business and community groups, including through processes such as working groups and roundtables

[256] Regulatory reform

[257] Australia will be among the most efficiently regulated places in the world, in the top five globally, reducing business costs by billions of dollars a year

[258] Pathways 

[259] Progress the six priority areas for major reform to lower costs for business and improve competition and productivity as agreed by the Council of Australian Governments (COAG) in April 2012. 13 

[260] Enter into a National Productivity Compact with the States and Territories and business to pursue regulatory and competition reform

[261] 

[262] Progress high-value reforms already identified by the Business Regulation and Competition Working Group and the Standing Council on Federal Financial Relations

[263] 

[264] Reduce reporting burdens on business by removing overlaps and expanding the use of online business reporting

[265] 

[266] Through COAG and processes such as the Business Advisory Forum, pursue continuous improvements to lift regulatory performance across all areas of regulatory practice, with a particular focus on the application of risk-based approaches and giving greater attention to reform implementation and enforcement

[267] Environmental sustainability

[268] The Australian economy and our environmental assets will be managed sustainably to ensure the wellbeing of future generations of Australians

[269] •

[270] Australia will have reduced emissions by at least 5 per cent below 2000 levels and we will be well on our way to securing a clean energy future in which emissions are 80 per cent below 2000 levels by

[271] •

[272] Australia will be a world leader in implementing sustainable food production methods, in sustainable energy and water use, and in biodiversity conservation

[273] Pathways 

[274] Fully implement our Clean Energy Future policies, alongside international action, to reduce Australia’s emissions intensity and absolute greenhouse gas emissions, through changes to the land sector, developing cleaner energy sources and linking with international carbon trading systems

[275] 

[276] Maintain our commitment to ensuring that 20 per cent of Australia’s electricity is generated by renewable energy sources by 2020. 

[277] Continue to support Australia being a world leader in the research and development of solar energy technologies, and becoming a world leader in the commercialisation and deployment of renewable energy technologies and energy efficiency

[278] 

[279] Achieve healthy rivers, strong communities and sustainable food production, including through finalising the Murray–Darling Basin Plan

[280] 

[281] Assess biodiversity impacts of growing demand for Australia’s non-renewable resources as part of the review of Australia’s Biodiversity Conservation Strategy 2010–2030 scheduled for

[282]  Implement the world’s largest marine reserve network and continue to protect Australia’s biodiversity on the land

[283] 

[284] Support the ongoing development and use of environmental accounting in Australia

[285] Macroeconomic and financial frameworks

[286] Australia’s macroeconomic and financial frameworks will remain among the world’s best through this period of change

[287] •

[288] Australia will have a strong and sustainable fiscal position and will continue to have a triple-A sovereign credit rating

[289] •

[290] Australia will have a deep and liquid corporate bond market to harness our national savings so that more investment is domestically funded and we have less reliance on offshore wholesale funding markets

[291] Pathways 

[292] Maintain the macroeconomic policy settings that have supported Australia’s long-term economic growth, including a floating exchange rate, independent monetary policy and a medium-term fiscal framework

[293] 

[294] Meet our fiscal targets of achieving budget surpluses, on average, over the medium term (including through maintaining a 2 per cent annual cap on real spending growth, on average, until surpluses are at least 1 per cent of GDP and while the economy is growing at or above trend) and improving the Government’s net worth over the medium term

[295] 

[561] Chapter 1: The rise of Asia Chapter 1: The rise of Asia Chapter 2: The future of Asia to 2025 Chapter 4: Outlook for Australia to 2025 Chapter 3: Australia in Asia The rise of Asia provides great opportunities for Australia • staggering scale and pace of rise • investment in people and capital • market and institutional reform • open global trading systems and stability • Asia has changed the world 29 Key points The pace and scale of Asia’s rise have been nothing short of staggering

[562] In a region rich in cultural, social, political and economic diversity, peoples’ lives have been transformed just as the globe has been transformed

[563] Hundreds of millions of people have been lifted out of poverty, parts of the region have experienced a halving in their infant mortality rates and decades have been added to life expectancy

[564] Nearly all the high-performing economies in Asia deliberately set out to support prosperity by reforming their policy and institutional settings

[565] Many economies within the region have invested heavily in their people and created a climate that has supported capital investments

[566] With the benefit of a good education, growing shares of young people have found jobs as they have reached prime working age

[567] Open global trading systems and infrastructure to reduce transport costs have driven regional and global integration

[568] More broadly, a global system of rules has allowed for greater stability and spurred increasing levels of interdependence

[569] Introduction Just over two decades ago, the Australian Government commissioned a study of Australia and the Northeast Asian ascendancy (Garnaut

[570] Since then, Asia has continued to change at an unprecedented pace and scale

[571] This White Paper looks at the group of nations that stretch from India through Southeast Asia to Northeast Asia, including Indonesia, other Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) members, China and Japan

[572] Asia is a region of great diversity—across ethnic groups, languages, history, institutions and natural endowments

[573] Its transformation into the world’s most dynamic economic region has been a defining development of our time

[574] Over the past 20 years, one-third of the world’s population has re-engaged with the global economy and more are set to do so (Chart

[575] Living standards for billions of people in Asia have improved at a rate not previously experienced in human history

[579] Between 2000 and 2006, around a million people were lifted out of poverty every week in East Asia alone (Gill & Kharas

[580] Japan, the Republic of Korea (South Korea), Singapore and, more recently, China and India doubled their income per person within a decade

[581] Some went on to repeat this achievement two or three times

[582] To put this into perspective, it took the United Kingdom over 50 years to double its income per person during the epoch-defining Industrial Revolution (Maddison

[583] This chapter looks at Asia’s success to date and how it has shaped the world

[584] Per cent Per cent Asia North America and Europe Rest of the world

[585] The makings of success Asia’s economic rise has been staggering, starting with Japan, whose emergence gathered pace from the 1950s

[586] The region’s success has not followed a single ‘recipe’

[587] Even where economies have drawn on the lessons of others, they have adapted approaches to suit their own circumstances and have implemented them alongside home-grown initiatives

[588] The region’s economies are diverse

[589] Some started their growth surge earlier; some have enjoyed greater success

[590] Incomes in Singapore, for example, are currently 12 times higher than in neighbouring Indonesia (Conference Board

[591] Economic progress has been uneven within countries too, including in the region’s large economies

[592] But amidst this diversity some common patterns have emerged in recent decades

[593] Nearly all the high-performing Asian economies deliberately set out to support prosperity by investing in people, building capital and undertaking institutional change, including expanding the role of markets

[594] With the benefits of a good education and employment-creating reforms, large numbers of young people have become productively employed as they reached prime working age, while a global system of rules has promoted stability and interdependence

[595] Open global trading systems and the construction of vital infrastructure to reduce transport costs have been drivers of integration

[596] Intricate regional production networks have emerged, along with increased flows of intermediate goods between regional partners

[597] Specialisation and scale have given the region a powerful advantage, particularly in manufactures

[598] Asia’s most successful economies have evolved continually in response to new developments

[599] As incomes have risen in population-dense economies such as Hong Kong, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, and as their labour-intensive activities have become less competitive, Asia’s high performers have refocused their production on new areas of consumer demand—developing domestic markets and specialising in high-skill activities

[600] Notwithstanding its diversity, the region is bound by a shared ambition for economic advancement

[601] The means may have varied, but the effort has been determined and the results staggering

[602] Asia’s demographic dividend In the early stages of their take-off, many economies in Asia faced a favourable set of circumstances as large numbers of young people approached working age, boosting the productive capacity of economies

[603] The region’s ability to capitalise on its favourable demographics has been a key factor underpinning Asia’s stellar income growth over the past four decades

[604] An East Asian baby boom, which started in Japan in the late 1940s, sparked a series of demographic and social changes that helped shape the region’s economic growth trajectory

[605] As the large ‘boom’ cohorts reached prime working and saving age (Chart 1.2), the productive capacity of economies such as Japan and South Korea expanded

[606] During this phase—from 1965 to 1990—East Asia’s working-age population grew nearly four times faster than its dependent population (Bloom & Williamson

[607] Chart 1.2: Asia’s demographic dividend Share of working-age population Source: UN (2011b

[608] Demography is not destiny

[609] Indeed, despite having experienced similar demographic transitions, Latin America as a whole was unable to achieve a demographic dividend in the 1960s to the 1990s (Bloom & Canning 2004, cited in Wei & Hao

[610] To take advantage of the favourable window provided by a youthful workforce, East Asian economies invested in physical capital, job training and technological progress

[611] With the benefits of a good education, East Asia’s large numbers of working-age people became a huge productive workforce

[612] Per cent Per cent Australia China Japan Malaysia Thailand 40 50 60 70 80 40 50 60 70 80 1950 1975 2000 2025 Per cent Per cent India Indonesia Philippines South Korea

[613] A virtuous spiral was created: population change increased income growth, and income growth pushed down population growth

[614] The consequent declines in fertility reduced youth dependency rates and further boosted women’s participation in the workforce

[615] East Asia’s ‘demographic dividend’ is estimated to have accounted for between one-quarter and two-fifths of its growth in GDP per person in the late 20th century.1 Favourable demographic changes were not confined to East Asia’s developed economies—other economies have also enjoyed a demographic dividend (Chart 1.2 and Box

[616] Between 1981 and 2010, the large share of working-age people is estimated to have boosted the growth rate of output per person by more than 1 per cent a year in Indonesia, South Korea, China, Thailand and Vietnam (ADB 2011b

[617] Box 1.1: Life has changed in Indonesia The experience of a child living in Indonesia tells the story of what has happened across large parts of Asia

[625] Now, the prospect of a city-based career in a professional service industry is a reality—and lifestyles are changing rapidly as a result

[626] Investing in people Asia’s young people enjoyed marked improvements in their access to education and its quality as governments invested in their youthful populations and dramatically transformed their education and training systems

[655] And the health of Vietnam’s women and children has improved substantially

[661] Jump-starting growth through investment As Asia’s economies emerged, they created a climate that supported investment— accelerating growth in the early stages of their development by rapidly investing in physical capital (Chart

[662] Higher levels of private and public investment enabled Asian countries to exploit their favourable demographics

[663] With access to better machinery and infrastructure, workers became more productive

[664] Technology and management systems, imported and adapted from overseas, further boosted productivity

[665] And as firms invested and 36 expanded their operations, competitive pressures on enterprises, including state-owned monopolies, lifted productivity

[666] The paths taken by Asian economies to stimulate investment have varied, but those that succeeded generally followed a two-pronged approach

[667] First, many built a favourable investment climate through a succession of—typically gradual and rudimentary—institution-building and market-enabling reforms

[668] Second, governments in successful Asian economies actively enabled and complemented markets in different ways that supported investment

[669] Different approaches ranged from putting in place export processing zones to various approaches to exchange rate management, and from industry-incentive arrangements to industry arm twisting

[670] Chart 1.4: Increasing investment in physical capital Gross fixed capital formation Note: The take-off years are 1990 for China, 1969 for Singapore, 1984 for South Korea and 1986 for Thailand (Hausmann et al

[671] Sources: World Bank (2012d) and Conference Board

[672] Institution-building and creating markets In the early phases of Asian countries’ rapid economic growth, institutional improvements helped create a favourable climate for human and physical capital accumulation

[673] Governments put in place more predictable property rights, opened up markets and invested in public goods such as basic knowledge, education and health

[674] Macroeconomic frameworks and governance more generally were improved

[675] Price controls were liberalised and production quotas were gradually removed

[676] Parts of previously closed economies were integrated into global markets, creating access to markets and finance, and boosting productivity

[677] Per cent of GDP Per cent of GDP Years after take-off China Singapore South Korea Thailand

[678] It was not just economic institutions that underwent change

[679] So did the formal and informal institutions that shape nations more broadly—governments and the military, the nature of political institutions and societal values and customs

[680] Countries across the region infused broad approaches to institutional improvement with their own unique practices

[681] Although its development followed that of many other economies in Asia, China in many ways epitomised the gradual and pragmatic approach to reform

[682] Its process is often described, in Chen Yun’s phrase, as ‘crossing the river by feeling stones’ (Li 1995 and Box

[683] Box 1.3: China—feeling the stones Reforms in China started in 1978 with the partial liberalisation of agriculture

[684] Those reforms allowed local farmers, rather than the state, to take responsibility for the profitability of their enterprises and gave them incentives by allowing them to sell produce above state-determined quotas

[685] In the 1980s, reforms also allowed largely communally owned enterprises to take advantage of new market opportunities— providing the engine of Chinese growth for two decades

[686] This was accompanied by the introduction and expansion of ‘special economic zones’, which provided concessions for private enterprise and foreign investment while the rest of the economy remained under controls and restrictions

[687] Over the next two decades, China continued its dual-track approach to reform as it encouraged private sector development while supporting state-owned enterprises in strategic industries

[688] It gradually liberalised price controls and sought to reform state-owned enterprises, financial markets and the housing sector

[689] China’s accession to the World Trade Organization (WTO) in 2001 was a further major step in integrating its economy with the global system

[690] Reforms that supported China’s commitment to the global trading system before its WTO accession should not be overlooked—no other member joining the WTO made so many concessions on the way to accession (Drysdale 2000; Brandt, Rawski & Zhu

[691] For example, in the decade before its accession to the WTO, China’s effective tariff rate halved to 15 per cent in 2000, and has since continued to fall (World Bank 2012d

[692] Combined with a governance structure that gave local and provincial governments incentives to experiment with different approaches to growing local economies, China was able to adapt institutions and settings to fit each stage of its development (World Bank & DRC

[693] Known as ‘township and village enterprises’

[694] Placing ownership in the hands of communities and local governments arguably struck a trade-off between lifting economic efficiency (by improving market incentives and property rights security) and ensuring that reform momentum was maintained by building constituencies and providing a ‘win–win’ for further reform (Qian

[695] Similar patterns of gradual reform are clear in the four small newly industrialised economies that have successfully made the transition to high-income economies

[696] Hong Kong, for example, took a liberal approach to economic development, setting itself up as a regional and global financial centre

[697] Singapore’s path was much more state-led

[698] Its distinctive brand of forward-looking public leadership, governance structures and investment in a high-performing public service allowed the country to take full advantage of its favourable geographical location

[699] South Korea and Taiwan used aggressive strategies to foster entrepreneurship and innovation and established themselves as technological powerhouses

[700] But as conditions change, so does the usefulness of existing institutions

[701] Over time, the region’s more successful economies have managed to adapt many institutions in response to changing conditions and challenges

[702] The benefits of investing in the formal institutions that support exchange increased as the Asian economies became richer, deeper and more complex

[703] It is this ability to maintain the pace of institutional reform that largely explains why some economies—including the highly developed Asian economies—have sustained their initial growth success to reach high-income status

[704] The reform path has not always been smooth

[705] For example, while the structure and practices of Japan’s financial sector were useful in initially driving rapid economic growth, they also contributed to the late-1980s asset bubble

[706] In response, Japan underwent a reform period focusing on corporate governance and the financial sector in the 1990s

[707] Similarly, the policy models that fuelled unprecedented economic growth in other countries and regions in Northeast and Southeast Asia contributed to asset price bubbles that later collapsed during the Asian financial crisis in 1997, which in turn required policy reform (Box

[708] 3

[709] For a discussion on the role of institutions in economic growth and development, see, for example, Zhuang, de Dios & Lagman-Martin (2010), Rodrik (2005), Aron (2000), Easterly (2005), Acemoglu & Robinson (2008) and North

[710] Box 1.4: The Asian financial crisis Several decades of unprecedented economic growth in many East and Southeast Asian economies came to an abrupt end in mid-1997 with the onset of the Asian financial crisis

[711] Their growth models, particularly the focus on large-scale mobilisation of investments, contributed to asset price bubbles that later burst, leading to capital flight, sharp currency movements and the abandonment of pegged exchange rates (Gill & Kharas

[712] Many factors lay behind the crisis and accounted for its severity: an inconsistent mix of macroeconomic and exchange rate policy settings, poor prudential supervision against a background of liberalisation of capital markets and underdeveloped domestic financial markets, lack of quick and coherent government action, and an overconfident international financial sector that had underestimated risks in the good years and panicked when economic conditions deteriorated

[713] The crisis had a devastating impact in several East Asian economies

[714] For instance, in 1998, Thailand’s real GDP fell by 8 per cent and Indonesia’s by 14 per cent

[715] Gross private financing to Asian emerging market economies collapsed from $128 billion in 1997 to $7 billion in

[716] Between 1996 and the second half of 1997, capital movements to Asia swung from annual inflows of almost $100 billion to outflows of the same size, while international bank loans to non-banks in Asia (excluding Japan) fell by more than $9 billion in the final quarter of 1997, the largest drop ever

[717] After the crisis, financial cooperation between ASEAN and East Asian economies became a regional priority, particularly through bodies such as ASEAN

[718] This was also a reaction to concerns that the International Monetary Fund (IMF) was dictating policy settings to the crisis-affected countries—Indonesia, South Korea and Thailand—in a manner the region thought to be both intrusive and inappropriate

[719] In the immediate aftermath of the crisis, Japan offered to underwrite an Asian monetary fund, triggering opposition from the United States and the IMF

[720] The proposal also lacked the support of China

[721] But it eventually led to what has become the Chiang Mai Initiative Multilateralisation, which started as a complex network of bilateral swap agreements and has since become a single, uniform facility to help with managing regional financial crises

[722] Reforms put in place since the Asian financial crisis have improved the resilience of Asian economies

[723] Openness, reliability and stability Asia’s rising economies were major beneficiaries of the open global trading system established under United States leadership after World War II

[724] In the early stages of their take-off, open global markets allowed them to take advantage of their large endowments of relatively unskilled, cheap labour

[725] In the most successful economies, early jobs in low-end manufactures, combined with hefty investments in education and training, enabled workers to learn the skills—and absorb and adapt advanced technology from abroad—that later permitted movement up the value-add chain (Krueger

[726] Regional efforts also supported greater levels of openness

[727] The Asia–Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum, for example, helped sustain market-driven integration in the region.4 More broadly, an open global trading regime enabled Asia’s rising economies to secure energy and resources vital to their growth, including from Australia

[728] This was particularly important for economies such as Japan and South Korea, which lacked large resource endowments

[729] At the same time, the security guarantees provided by the United States to its key allies in the region, especially Japan and South Korea, and the development of an effective working relationship between Washington and Beijing after 1972, provided strategic (and business) confidence that helped frame and support the region’s economic development

[730] The post–Cold War consolidation of ASEAN to incorporate the countries of Indochina helped establish the foundations for Southeast Asia’s development

[731] Asia has changed the world As Asia has grown over the past two decades, it has changed the world

[732] Asia’s impact on global markets has been profound

[733] More regional and global firms have emerged from Asia to shape the way businesses operate across the globe

[734] The region’s industrialisation and urbanisation have sparked demand for raw materials, creating a resources boom

[735] And Asia’s burgeoning middle class has reshaped global markets, including for high-value consumer goods and services—spanning everything from electronics to tourism

[736] Average tariffs of APEC members have declined from 16 per cent in 1989 to around 6 per cent in

[737] Asia has shifted global production, trade and investment With the emergence of ‘Factory Asia’, Asia has become the production engine for the world (Chart

[738] As it has done so, it has also transformed the way the world produces goods and services

[741] Integrated parts of the production process have spread across several different countries

[742] These cross-border value chains first developed for cars and electronics and had their genesis in Japan’s economic rise

[743] As Japan developed, its production costs rose and the yen appreciated

[744] Japanese companies began specialising in higher skill goods and services in Japan, while moving parts of their labour-intensive assembly operations to South Korea, Hong Kong, Taiwan and Singapore

[745] As production costs rose in these economies, businesses relocated assembly processes to ASEAN countries and then to China; China quickly became the main assembly plant for Factory Asia

[746] India, however, has so far followed a different economic development path from that of East Asia (Box

[751] India’s information technology, business services and financial services industries— the modern services sector—have recently been powering services exports

[752] Their share in India’s services export earnings has more than doubled over the past decade, to around 19 per cent in

[753] Software exports now rival India’s other major services export—income from international ‘guest’ labour

[755] There are signs of improvement and elements of manufacturing are already globally competitive

[756] For example, India’s automotive and automotive components sector has thrived on the back of foreign investment, strong growth in domestic incomes and vibrant export opportunities

[757] In 2010–11, more than 17 million vehicles were produced, most of which were ‘two-wheelers’

[758] India’s automotive sector now accounts for more than 5 per cent of GDP and directly employs more than 5 million workers

[759] India has recognised the need to make substantial investments in skills and infrastructure to better equip India’s future workforce and improve its competitiveness

[760] Boosting industrial activity and employment is the driving impetus behind its 2011 National Manufacturing Policy

[761] East Asia now accounts for almost one-third of world trade in manufacturing, and the intermediate goods trade accounts for more than half of all interregional trade in East Asia

[763] Now the world’s largest exporter, China’s share of global value-add manufacturing has doubled over the past decade

[764] Not all parts of Asia have formed deep economic ties with their immediate neighbours

[765] Links within South Asia have been growing, but they are still relatively modest

[766] These links have been constrained by political tension (despite some promise of change), poor physical connectivity and impediments to cross-border trade and investment

[767] More recently, Asia’s emergence has also reshaped global financial markets

[768] Over the past decade, regional investment has expanded rapidly and regional financial markets have become closer and more efficient as economies have become more interdependent

[769] And in the decade before the Global Financial Crisis in 2008, 43 Asia also financed high rates of investment in developed economies—supporting growth in the United States and Europe

[770] While portfolio flows have oscillated, Asia has become a major net exporter of capital to the rest of the world through both growing foreign exchange reserves and private investment flows

[771] Asia’s foreign exchange reserves over the past decade have soared, with about two-thirds of the world’s accumulated reserves in 2012 (Bloomberg

[772] China and Japan were the main contributors, at about one-third and one-tenth of global reserves respectively, but the pattern of accumulation has been common across countries in the region (Gill & Kharas

[773] But, despite the region’s impressive progress to strengthen financial systems and build regional connections, Asian financial markets remain relatively underdeveloped and are more closely linked to global markets than to each other

[774] Asia’s rapid growth and urbanisation have transformed global commodity markets Urbanisation has transformed Asian societies

[775] Urbanisation in Asia involves around 44 million people—around twice the size of Australia’s current population—leaving rural areas and being added to the population of cities every year in search of opportunities

[776] The impacts have been staggering

[777] Between 1990 and 2009, energy consumption in Asia more than doubled and the region’s share of global energy consumption increased from 25 to 38 per cent (IEA

[778] Demand has not been limited to energy

[779] Between 2001 and 2011, iron ore prices increased by a factor of 13, zinc prices more than doubled, and copper, lead and tin prices all increased at least fivefold (IMF 2012c

[780] This process—along with the region’s rapid growth, massive infrastructure investment and ongoing industrialisation—has boosted demand for a broad range of mineral and energy resources (Chart 1.6), affecting all resource-supplying nations, including Australia

[781] With its rapid growth, intensive resource use and sheer scale, China has led the pack

[782] It is now the world’s largest energy consumer, having gone from consuming less than half as much energy as the United States in 2000, to consuming slightly more today (IEA

[786] China’s growth and technological change have also demanded lesser-known materials

[787] Demand has increased for manganese (used in the production of stainless steel), antimony (electronics), scandium (aluminium alloys) and zircon (ceramic glazes

[832] Asia’s growing weight is altering the focus of global governance Finally, Asia is not a self-contained strategic or economic system

[833] The rising influence of emerging economies in Asia is shifting the focus of global governance

[834] The formation of the Group of Twenty (G20) following the Asian financial crisis— particularly its elevation to a leader level forum in 2008—is an example

[835] Changes to the governance and membership of rules-setting bodies such as the International Monetary Fund (IMF) have also begun

[836] An important sign of the shift in financial relativities was the substantial commitment that emerging economies made to the IMF’s crisis reserves at the G20 summit in Mexico in

[837] ASEAN has consolidated its role in the evolving regional architecture

[839] Chapter 2: The future of Asia to 2025 Chapter 1: The rise of Asia Chapter 2: The future of Asia to 2025 Chapter 4: Outlook for Australia to 2025 Chapter 3: Australia in Asia The rise of Asia provides great opportunities for Australia • strong income growth ahead • shifting trade and consumption patterns • competition for resources • prosperity through stability 49 Key points Asia’s past cannot be explained by a single model; nor will its future be a single destiny, but there are good reasons to be optimistic

[840] While the shape of the Asian century is not set in stone, the scale and pace of Asia’s rise in the coming decades is expected to be staggering

[841] Many nations in the region have only just begun to catch up to the productivity levels enjoyed in advanced economies, promising strong income growth for decades to come

[842] Asia will not just be the most populous region in the world

[843] Asia will be the biggest economic zone, the biggest consumption zone and the home to the majority of the world’s middle class

[844] Economic cycles affecting the region are expected to occur around a rising long-term income trend

[845] The economies and societies of Asia will transform as they become more prosperous

[846] Over the coming decades, the nations of Asia will face new pressures, including likely moderate economic growth among advanced-economy trading partners, greater competition for natural resources and further environmental constraints

[847] Despite substantial declines in poverty levels, rising income disparities will challenge social stability

[848] And Asia’s continued growth won’t occur in a strategic vacuum

[849] Stable relations among the major powers in Asia and the Pacific—China, India, Indonesia, Japan and the United States—will remain fundamental to prosperity and security in the region and will require sustained effort

[850] Each nation’s choices about its own institutions and policies will guide its future growth and prosperity, as will global economic and other developments

[912] With few exceptions, economies in Asia have been rapidly catching up with the productivity levels of more advanced economies

[913] They have introduced markets to allocate resources efficiently, harnessed domestic savings for capital investment, and adopted existing technologies and foreign investment to create productivity growth

[914] A few, of course, have already reached, or are close to, the global technological frontier

[915] But the fruits of adopting new technology and adapting it will become harder to harvest

[916] A point will come, though it’s still some way off, where the growth of labour productivity in developing Asian economies will slow—opportunities for gains from importing foreign technology and for shifting workers from agriculture to industry will diminish

[917] High levels of capital investment have been a considerable support for labour productivity growth in the region, but the next phase of such growth will likely draw from a wider set of sources—including investment in skills and education, further urbanisation, capitalising on further opportunities for deeper integration into the global economy and the rapid growth of other emerging economies

[918] The outlook for Asia is optimistic and it is shifting the global economy While the shape of the Asian century is not set in stone, there are good reasons to be optimistic

[961] But Asia’s development has not been evenly distributed Although the conditions of Asia’s poor have improved markedly, the incomes of the rich have been growing at a faster rate

[962] Gaps have widened along rural-urban, gender and ethnic lines

[963] Cities and coastal areas were the first to benefit from Asia’s integration and development, while interior regions have lagged

[964] Wide disparities now exist between the coastal and inland provinces in China, the eastern, southern and western states in India, and western and eastern Indonesia

[967] In India, the wage premium is more than 30 per cent

[968] Urban incomes in China are two and a half times those in rural areas

[1121] Projected sea-level rise, more intense tropical storms and higher wind speeds could inundate low-lying port cities, threaten coastal areas, exacerbate flooding and increase the salinity of rivers and bays across the region

[1131] If the region is to reach its potential, it must address its growing food, energy, water and climate constraints

[1132] Significant efforts to do so are already underway

[1133] But for them to succeed, the region must avoid past approaches, where attempts to fix one area without regard for effects elsewhere led to unintended consequences

[1134] The links between food, water, energy and climate change are multiple and fundamental, and so a whole-of-system approach to these challenges is critical

[1135] Growing demand for food Asia’s demand for food commodities is set to grow

[1136] In order to feed a larger, more urban and richer population, food production in 2050 needs to be around 70 per cent higher than today

[1137] Most of the projected increase in food demand will come from Asia (Linehan et al

[1138] The shift towards more protein-rich food and a wider variety of vegetables and fruit, combined with growth in biofuels, will also be more resource intensive

[1139] The world is expected to be able to achieve the required increase in food production (FAO 2009; World Bank 2009), mostly from higher yields and cropping intensity

[1140] But meeting the required increase in food production will not come easily

[1141] While the increase needed in agricultural yields is comparable to those achieved in the past, crop productivity growth is slowing and producers face much greater environmental constraints and challenges than before

[1142] And in many areas, climate change is multiplying these challenges

[1143] By 2030, rising sea levels could expose large parts of the Mekong Delta to extreme salinisation and crop damage

[1144] The focus on lifting agricultural productivity will need to extend beyond the farm gate

[1145] Investments in water and transport infrastructure, particularly roads, irrigation systems and dams, will also be required

[1146] Such investments would help farmers better integrate into value chains and markets as well as help reduce food loss and waste

[1147] A lack of hard infrastructure, such as storage and cooling facilities and transportation, means that food does not always make it to market

[1148] The combination of resource and environmental constraints, along with higher input costs, will constrain the supply response in most regions, so coming decades will be characterised by high food prices

[1149] Stronger links between agricultural and energy markets, as well as more frequent extreme weather shocks, will also add to food price volatility

[1150] Water scarcity is set to increase Meeting the region’s growing food demands will be complicated by water scarcity

[1151] Asia is a relatively water-scarce region, and the complexity and scale of its water problems are set to grow

[1152] Growing populations and cities, changing diets and expanding energy and industrial production will demand greater shares of the region’s limited water resources

[1153] Industrial water use alone is projected to increase by 65 per cent by 2030, crowding out growth in agricultural water use (ADB 2011d

[1154] 71

[1156] In developing Asia, aggregate water shortfalls could reach 40 per cent, with implications for the region’s food and energy production, its ecological needs and the health and livelihoods of its population

[1247] In the post-war period, Asia’s commitment to internationally oriented development opened unprecedented new opportunities for the resource-abundant Australian economy

[1248] Australia’s economic integration into Asia has accelerated over the past four decades

[1249] Steps to open up the Australian economy began in the 1970s with landmark tariff cuts in

[1250] Comprehensive reforms to Australia’s economic institutions and frameworks then gathered pace from the mid-1980s

[1251] These reforms and Australia’s more recent successful response to the Global Financial Crisis have laid the foundation for Australians to benefit from the opportunities stemming from the region—such as the surge in resource demand and the rising middle class in Asia—with the gains of success spread across the nation

[1252] More recent policy reforms—including in tax, regulation, skills, school funding, managing the resources boom, increasing connectivity and investing in infrastructure—are important components of our agenda to further strengthen the economy’s resilience and diversity and enhance our ability to engage with Asia

[1253] Cultural diversity is at the centre of Australia’s identity

[1254] The face of Australia has changed dramatically in recent decades and Asia is now an important part of our identity

[1255] The Australian Government is engaging more with regional partners through multilateral institutions, regional forums and bilateral exchanges

[1256] Australia has built deep and broad relationships within the region, across educational, cultural and social dimensions

[1257] Our people-to-people connections with Asia have deepened and have transformed our society

[1258] Introduction Australia’s interactions with nations in Asia have shaped our strategic focus and the structure of our economy and society

[1259] In the early decades after Federation in 1901, Australia’s mindset was oriented mainly towards the British Empire and Europe

[1260] Following World War II, Australia shifted its strategic focus to the United States and countries closer to home

[1261] And over time Australia’s economic focus also has shifted into the region

[1262] Over the past four decades, Australia has transformed its economy, society and institutions as it has become closer to Asia

[1263] Asia’s commitment to modernisation and internationally oriented development opened unprecedented new opportunities for Australia to become a highly productive and reliable supplier of resources and related goods and services to the region and the world

[1264] Our economic integration with Asia gathered pace as our economic settings were liberalised

[1265] Our people-to-people connections with Asia have transformed our society through migration, business, travel, study and popular culture

[1266] Developing institutional connections Successive generations have transformed Australia from a nation that once built defensive walls to shield itself from the region and the globe into an open, outward looking, prosperous society, securing its future in the region

[1267] Australian interactions with the Asian region have a long history, dating back to contact between Indonesian fishermen from Makassar and Indigenous communities in northern Australia before European settlement, and early migration from a number of Asian regions during the colonial period

[1268] But all the elements of what has been described as the ‘Australian Settlement’ that underpinned Federation—’White Australia, industry protection, wage arbitration, state paternalism and imperial benevolence’ (Kelly 1992)—had the effect of stunting the relationship with Asia

[1269] In the early decades after Federation, Australia’s economic, political and strategic mindsets were oriented mainly towards the British Empire and Europe

[1270] While there was an awareness of Asia, and cultural, economic and diplomatic exchanges with countries in the region took place, their development was constrained by Australian institutions

[1271] This reflected the values and attitudes of a time when many Australians defined themselves as distant and separate from Asia

[1272] World War II was a major strategic shock for Australia

[1273] The fall of Singapore in 1942 marked a new chapter

[1274] Australia shifted its attention squarely to Asia and developed a security partnership with the United States

[1275] See Stokes (2004) for a critique of that summary and an alternative formulation

[1276] 79

[1277] In the immediate post-war period, Australian policy towards Asia was driven mainly by political, defence and security considerations, particularly decolonisation and its implications for Asian security, and the regional manifestations of the Cold War

[1278] After World War II, the Chifley government was engaged in laying the foundations for a new international order, in which the United Nations was envisaged as playing a central role

[1279] Australia lent strong diplomatic support for independence for Indonesia, Myanmar, India, Pakistan, the Philippines and Sri Lanka

[1280] Successive Australian governments took the view that Australia should contribute to the region through development assistance

[1281] Conceived under the Chifley Government, and established under the Menzies Government in 1951, Australia led in the development of the Colombo Plan, offering scholarships whose recipients included a significant number of emerging Asian leaders

[1282] The rapprochement with Japan in the 1950s, driven by the signing of the Agreement of Commerce in 1957, was a catalyst for Australia establishing itself as Asia’s premier resources supplier and accelerated the shift of Australian diplomatic focus to the region

[1283] Meanwhile, the Cold War reinforced Australia’s preoccupation with sustaining major power (notably United States) military and wider engagement in the region

[1284] The conclusion of the ANZUS Treaty in 1951, which cemented our US alliance, was a landmark

[1285] Australia also encouraged the United Kingdom to retain its military and wider influence in the region into the 1970s

[1286] These strategic considerations lay behind Australian policy in relation to Vietnam, including the decision to deploy Australian armed forces there

[1287] They were also prominent in Australia’s decision to support Malaysia diplomatically and militarily when it was facing threats from the Sukarno government in Indonesia during the confrontation (Konfrontasi) period

[1288] A distinctive feature of the 1950s was the expansion of Australian diplomatic representation in the region

[1289] Richard Casey, as External Affairs Minister, led this effort to build relations with the region

[1290] By 1960, when he retired from this role, Australia had established diplomatic missions in 14 Asian countries (Gifford

[1291] One of Australia’s distinctive contributions to the region has been to encourage more effective mechanisms for political, strategic and economic consultation and cooperation

[1292] Australia, under the Whitlam Government, became the first external dialogue partner of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) in 1974 and has participated regularly in the ASEAN Post Ministerial Conference, which brings together ASEAN and its dialogue partners, including Australia, once a year

[1293] Economic ties with the region deepened and broadened under the Hawke and Keating governments, with Australia playing a central role, alongside Japan and South Korea, in the development of the Asia–Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum in the late 1980s and early 1990s

[1294] Although APEC’s agenda is largely economic, it helped 80 foster positive habits of cooperation and consultation and a stronger sense of shared regional interests

[1295] Until the recent formation of the East Asia Summit, annual APEC leaders’ meetings were the only forum to bring together the heads of government of most regional economies

[1296] Working closely with regional partners, notably Indonesia, Australia has encouraged the development of broadly inclusive regional security mechanisms like the ASEAN Regional Forum in 1994 and the ASEAN Defence Ministers’ Meeting-Plus in

[1297] We have supported informal networks and processes such as the Pacific Economic Cooperation Council and the Council for Security Cooperation in the Asia–Pacific network of think tanks and academics

[1298] In addition to their functional importance, these processes have helped develop extensive personal networks of ministers, officials, businesspeople, academics and other experts around the region

[1299] Regional and global institutions, like these, continue to evolve partly in response to Asia’s rise

[1300] Australia has a growing engagement with regional partners in multilateral organisations

[1301] It has been at the forefront of support for reforms to international institutions to reflect the increasing importance of emerging economies

[1304] The Group of Twenty (G20) gives us close engagement with China, Japan, India, Indonesia and South Korea

[1305] Australia and our regional partners have established strong frameworks for practical cooperation to address shared regional security and related challenges

[1311] A further, longstanding strand in Australia’s engagement with Asia has been our development cooperation program

[1313] Australian development assistance focuses on poverty alleviation and assisting the most vulnerable

[1314] It helps countries connect with the economic dynamism in Asia in a self-sustaining way by building skills and capacity, strengthening institutions and governance, and supporting sustainability

[1315] Economic links are another major feature of Australian engagement with the region

[1316] Our economic ties became more important in the late 1950s

[1317] The 1957 Commerce Agreement between Australia and Japan started a boom in our economic ties and growing recognition that Australia’s future lay in the region (Drysdale

[1318] Australia was a reliable supplier to other Asian nations as well (for example, Australia exported wheat to China during the Cold War

[1320] The Whitlam Government’s recognition of the People’s Republic of China in 1972 and the establishment of diplomatic ties was a milestone

[1322] The 1997 Asian financial crisis reinforced Australia’s growing economic interdependence with Asia

[1323] Australia was active in responding to the crisis, joining Japan and other countries to support arrangements to assist Indonesia, South Korea and Thailand

[1329] How our economy transformed alongside Asia’s Australia’s economic institutions inherited at Federation stood unchallenged, and indeed were extended, in the decades immediately after World War II

[1330] The growth strategy in the seven decades after Federation resulted in an economy that was overregulated and underproductive

[1331] On a number of occasions, Australia’s inflexible macroeconomic settings buckled under the strain of global economic forces

[1332] Households and businesses that were not sheltered by our version of mercantilism were being short changed by a succession of failures in Australia’s winner-picking policies
